For most of recorded human history, the written word was a luxury good—laboriously copied by hand, guarded by institutions, and accessible only to a tiny elite. The emergence of mechanical printing in the fifteenth century shattered that arrangement and set in motion a cascade of transformations that reshaped religion, science, politics, and the very texture of daily life. # From Woodblock to Rotary: A History of the Printing Press

The history of the printing press is, in many ways, the history of how knowledge escaped its confinement. For most of recorded history, the written word was the preserve of a tiny elite—scribes, priests, and scholars who controlled the slow, painstaking reproduction of texts by hand. The emergence of mechanical printing in the fifteenth century shattered that monopoly and set in motion transformations that would reshape religion, science, politics, and culture across the globe. What follows traces that long arc: from the earliest inked impressions on paper in East Asia, through Gutenberg's revolutionary synthesis in Europe, to the industrial behemoths of the nineteenth century and the eventual displacement of metal type by photographic and digital technologies. It is a story of technical ingenuity, but also of commerce, censorship, revolution, and the ceaseless human desire to multiply the word.

# The History of the Printing Press: From Woodblock to Revolution

The history of the printing press is, in many ways, the history of how knowledge became public. For most of human history, the written word was a scarce commodity, guarded by elites and produced at enormous cost. The emergence of mechanized printing in the fifteenth century shattered that monopoly and set in motion transformations that would reshape religion, politics, science, and culture across the globe. To trace the story of the printing press is to trace the story of modernity itself—its liberations and its upheavals alike.

## Precursors: Writing, Paper, and Early Reproduction

Long before movable type appeared in Europe, societies had developed sophisticated methods for reproducing texts. The invention of paper in China around the second century CE provided an essential substrate; without affordable paper, mass printing would have been impossible. By the Tang dynasty, Chinese artisans were carving entire pages into wooden blocks, inking them, and pressing them onto paper—a technique known as woodblock printing. The earliest dated printed book, a copy of the Diamond Sutra from 868 CE, survives from this tradition. Woodblock printing spread to Korea and Japan, where it was used for Buddhist texts, calendars, and later for popular literature.
